Chapter 3: Violence as a Constant Shadow
For the boys growing up here, violence isn’t just something that happens now and then—it’s part of their everyday world. Imagine hearing gunshots in the distance, spotting police cars on your block, and always knowing that danger could show up at any moment. For them, fear just becomes part of life.
The older brother? He’s learned how to read the streets like a map. He knows which corners to cross, who to avoid, and exactly when to keep his head down. He’s seen what happens when you get caught in the wrong place at the wrong time. Friends have been hurt, some have vanished, and everyone knows someone who’s been taken by the streets.
The younger brother, though, still has a little bit of innocence left. He keeps asking questions—maybe too many—trying to make sense of why things are the way they are. He’s watched fights start out of nowhere, seen arguments suddenly turn deadly, and felt the tension in the air when things go quiet. He’s learned to run when trouble starts, and to hide when he needs to.
Their mother worries all the time. She tries to keep her sons close, hoping she can keep them safe from the worst of it. But she knows she can’t protect them from everything. She’s watched too many families break apart, too many young lives end way too soon. She talks to her boys about being careful, about making good choices, but deep down, she knows that sometimes, even that isn’t enough.
The violence isn’t just something you see or feel—it gets inside you, too. The boys carry the weight of everything they’ve witnessed. There’s always that fear: what if something happens to them, or to someone they care about? It changes how they look at the world, how much they trust, and even how they picture their future. Some days, it feels like hope is slipping away, and all that’s left is a hard edge that wasn’t there before.
Most people don’t realize just how exhausting it is to always be alert—to constantly watch your back. The boys learn to move fast, to keep their eyes sharp, to sense when something’s off. They find their own ways to cope—maybe by joking around, leaning on friends, or dreaming of a life somewhere else. Still, the scars stick with them, shaping who they are and who they might become.
And yet, even with all this, there are moments that break through the darkness. Neighbors look out for each other, share warnings, and watch the kids. The boys find comfort in the little routines, and in the familiar faces that remind them they’re not alone. Even in all the chaos, there are flashes of hope—proof that life, even here, is about more than just surviving.
